A longitudinal study followed 2,400 adults for eight years to examine whether remote work affects social isolation. Participants completed quarterly surveys measuring loneliness, friendship frequency, and perceived community support, while researchers controlled for baseline extroversion, income, and prior mental health diagnoses. The average change in loneliness was small, but the distribution was wide: caregivers and new hires reported increased isolation, while experienced workers with flexible schedules reported slight improvements. The study cautions against simple averages because selection effects matter—people who choose remote roles may differ systematically from those who cannot. The authors infer that remote work is not inherently isolating; outcomes depend on job autonomy, life stage, and intentional social routines, suggesting targeted interventions rather than one-size-fits-all mandates.
